built.by: citadel of the City of the Four Regions (regal period); sentinels posted here during comitia in the Campus Martius (Cass. Dio 37.28); held against the Gauls 390 BC (Livy 5.47); M. Manlius Capitolinus's house stood here until destroyed in 384 BC (Livy 6.20.13)

monuments.english: Arx (citadel, northern summit of the Capitol)

Marcellus 222 BC (Liv. Per. 20; Plut. Marc. 8). Augustus's restoration: P&A 'probably about 31 BC' (Nep. Att. 20.3; Mon. Anc. 4.5 = RG 19.2; Liv. 4.20.7), so the event year here is 31, not 32.

built.by: vowed by L. Furius Purpurio as praetor in the Gallic war of 200 (Livy 31.21.12, emended text); dedicated by the duumvir Q. Marcius Ralla in 192 (Livy 35.41.8, emended text); P&A treats the identification as unsettled

monuments.form: cella wider than deep with pronaos columns added along the flanks (Vitr. 4.8.4); cult statue of a youthful god with arrows and a goat (Gell. 5.12.11; Ov. Fast. 3.443); travertine/tufa remains survive below the Tabularium
monuments.geometry_source: form assumed from date and type, native kit size (no measured plan); Platner-Ashby s.v. Vediovis, Aedes (cella wider than deep, unusual orientation: not read, not reproduced)

monuments.notes: CORRECTED. P&A treats two temples of Vediovis. (1) On the Tiber island, known only from an emended text of Liv. 34.53.7 (194 BC: dedicated by the duumvir C. (2) The Capitoline temple 'inter duos lucos' (Vitr. 4.8.4; Gell. 5.12.5), dedicated on 7 March (Ov. Fast. 3.429-430): Liv. 35.41.8 (192 BC) says Q. Marcius Ralla, duumvir, dedicated a temple vowed by Purpurio, but the MSS read 'aedes duae Iovi' and the emendation to Vediovis is conjectural. P&A says the matter cannot be settled. The previous entry's 'contracted 194; dedicated 192 (Livy 34.53.7)' mixed the island temple with the Capitoline one. Livy 31.21.12 is the vow of 200 (MSS 'deo Iovi'). built.by: vowed by the praetor T. Otacilius Crassus in 217 after Lake Trasimene on the Sibylline books' advice (Livy 22.9.10, 22.10.10); dedicated by Otacilius as duumvir in 215 (Livy 23.31.9, 23.32.20), on 8 June (Ov. Fast. 6.247-248)

built.by: vowed by the dictator Q. Fabius Maximus in 217 after Lake Trasimene on the Sibylline books' advice (Livy 22.9.7-10, 22.10.10); dedicated by Fabius as duumvir in 215 (Livy 23.30.13-14, 23.31.9)

Porcius Ligustinus there), dedicated by his son L. Porcius Licinus as duumvir in 181 BC. Site: outside the Porta Collina, probably west of the Via Salaria near the modern Via Belisario (P&A); precision rough. Strabo 6.2.6 says it was a copy of the temple at Eryx with a noteworthy portico. Festivals 23 April (Vinalia) and 24 October.

built.by: Numa's shrine (Livy 1.21.4; Dion. Hal. 2.75); temple dedicated by A. Atilius Calatinus in 254 or 250 BC (Cic. Nat. D. 2.61), on 1 October (fasti)

D. 2.61), restored and re-dedicated by M. Aemilius Scaurus in 115; dedication day 1 October. Used for Senate meetings (Val. Max. 3.17; App. BC 1.16) and held treaty tablets. Probably in the south-east corner of the Area Capitolina near the Porta Pandana; exact site unknown.

built.by: valley drained by sewers (cloacae) under Tarquinius Priscus and plots round the forum assigned for porticoes and shops (Livy 1.38.6); the first open area with a fixed level at 10.60-10.90 m above sea level dates probably to the 6th c. BC (P&A)

events.what: great fire destroys the shops and houses round the Forum; later rebuilt (Livy 26.27.1-4)
a new, higher level (c. 174 BC) in the Comitium; the censors of 174 had the Capitoline slope and streets paved (Livy 41.27.5-7; level date from P&A)
funeral of Clodius: Curia Hostilia burned (Asc. Mil. 29-33; Cic. Mil. 90; Dio 40.49)

P&A: the first open area with fixed limits is marked by cappellaccio pavements at 10.60-10.90 m above sea level (c. 6th c.); a new level c. 174 BC; a level attributed to Sulla (Van Deman, uncertain); the Cloaca Maxima credited to the Tarquins (excavations support a 6th-c. date). Livy 26.27.1-4 is the fire of 210 (verified). The plot of land is Pleiades 502866838 (archaeological site; its representative point is about 120 m ESE of the plaza centre used here).

built.by: open place of assembly connected with the Curia from the regal period (Livy 1.36.5; Varro LL 5.155); its levels date from the 6th century BC (P&A)

events.what: debris of buildings burned in the Gallic fire lies under the second level of the Comitium (P&A)

monuments.form: open templum, orientated to the cardinal points, with the Curia on its north side, the Rostra and Graecostasis on the south and the Carcer and Basilica Porcia on the west; five successive levels excavated
monuments.geometry_source: Platner-Ashby s.v. Comitium (circular, rostra vetera on the south edge facing due south, levels 10.4-13.5 m); radius from the Comitium steps, not measured in PA
monuments.location: north-west corner of the Forum, below the Curia; round-ish open space for assemblies
monuments.notes: Not in Pleiades. P&A: the Comitium was an open, inaugurated templum (Cic. Rep. 2.11), oriented to the cardinal points, with the Curia on the north side, the Carcer and Basilica Porcia on the west, the Rostra and Graecostasis on the south; five successive levels from c. 390 (after the Gallic fire) to the Caesarian travertine/marble pavement. It was the political centre until the 2nd c. BC; C. Licinius Crassus (tribune 145) first led the assembly from the Comitium to the Forum (Cic. Lael. 25, 96; Varro RR 1.2.9). Faustus Sulla's travertine pavement (12.63 m) is attributed to his restoration after 52 BC. The earlier claim that Sulla 'levelled and rebuilt' the Comitium in 80 BC is not in P&A (it only says Sulla restored the Curia and Rostra) and has been replaced. Dio 43.49.1 not checked here against Dio.

built.by: archaic sanctuary with inscribed cippus (c. 500 BC), sacellum probably later 4th c. BC; black marble paving laid over it in the Caesarian reconstruction of the Comitium (c. 45 BC) (P&A); Festus 184L: 'niger lapis in comitio locum funestum significat', variously linked to Romulus's death or burial

monuments.geometry_source: black marble paving in the Comitium, about 3.5 x 4 m (Platner-Ashby s.v. Lapis Niger: not read for dimensions)
monuments.location: Comitium, in front of the Curia
monuments.notes: CORRECTED: P&A (s.v. Sepulcrum Romuli; 'Niger Lapis: see Sepulcrum Romuli') describes a black pavement of marmor Taenarium about 4 x 3 m, found 1899 in front of the Curia Iulia and lying on the level of the Caesarian pavement of the Comitium, covering an archaic cippus with inscription (dated c. 500 BC), a tufa cone (5th c.) and a 'sacellum' (probably later 4th c.). So the black paving is of Caesar's time (c. 45 BC), not 'c. 80 BC'; the shrine below is archaic. Festus 184L = p. 177 in Muller's pagination (P&A). Dion. Hal. does not give the Lapis Niger passage here; the cited 'Dion. Hal. 3.?' was removed. Pleiades 326532998 (precise).

built.by: platform of the Comitium decorated with the beaks (rostra) of the ships taken from Antium by C. Maenius in 338 (Livy 8.14.12; Pliny NH 34.20); platform itself older (mid 5th c. low platform, rebuilt higher after 390: P&A)

events.what: restored by Sulla (P&A)

Name from the beaks of the Antium ships, 338 BC (Pliny NH 34.20; Livy 8.14.12). Restored by Sulla; moved by Caesar to the north-west end of the Forum (Suet. Aug. 100 'rostra veteres'; Dio 43.49.1). Livy 8.14.12 verified in the Latin text.

Rostra Augusti)
monuments.geometry_source: Platner-Ashby s.v. Rostra Augusti (read): front about 24 m long and 3 high, platform 10 m deep from the western wall, curved steps on the west (about 4 m assumed); point of the remains as in the dataset's Rostra entry; faces the Forum (ESE)

built.by: begun by Caesar in 44 to replace the Curia Hostilia (Dio 44.5.2), continued by the triumvirs (Dio 45.17, 47.19); completed and dedicated by Octavian in 29 (Dio 51.22.1; Res Gestae 19.1)

built.by: dedication ascribed to the first years of the Republic: T. Larcius as dictator (501, Macrob. Sat. 1.8.1), begun 498 (Dion. Hal. 6.1.4), dedicated 497 (Livy 2.21.2); other traditions credit Tullus Hostilius or the last Tarquin (Varro)

events.what: porticus built from the temple along the Clivus Capitolinus to the Capitol (Livy 41.27.7)
rebuilt by L. Munatius Plancus (Suet. Aug. 29)

monuments.form: temple at the foot of the Capitoline hill on the Clivus Capitolinus, housing the state treasury (aerarium); blocks of the original podium and an early stone-arched drain survive; the eight standing columns (11 m high, granite) belong to the 4th-century AD restoration
monuments.geometry_source: Platner-Ashby s.v. Saturnus, Aedes (podium 22.50 m wide, about 40 long; Ionic hexastyle prostyle, columns 11 m high; Plancus phase drawn as the kit Ionic hexastyle); front faces the Forum (east); archaic phase small Tuscan
monuments.location: west end of the Forum, at the foot of the Capitol (Clivus Capitolinus); the Aerarium was in its podium
monuments.notes: No Pleiades place for the Temple of Saturn found in the Pleiades dump. P&A: dedication tradition varies: Tullus Hostilius, begun by the last Tarquin, or dedicated by T. Larcius as dictator in 501 (Macrob. 1.8.1; Dion. Hal. 6.1.4 says begun 498 in Larcius's second consulship); P&A says the dedication 'may safely be assigned to the beginning of the republic'. Livy 2.21.2 (497 BC, consuls A. Sempronius and M. Minucius) is the usual year. Dedication day: Saturnalia, 17 December. 174 BC: porticus built from the temple up the Clivus Capitolinus (Liv. 41.27.7). Rebuilt by L. Munatius Plancus in 42 (Suet. Aug. 29). Standing columns (8, granite) are a 4th-c. AD restoration. The state treasury (aerarium) was in it; the Tabularium (78) took over some records. Original podium blocks survive.

temple_octastyle_peripteral.source: Platner-Ashby s.v. Castor, Aedes (read): Corinthian, octastyle peripteral, eleven columns on each side, the whole about 50 x 30 m, the floor about 7 m above the Sacra Via; columns of white marble, fluted, 12.50 m high and 1.45 thick, entablature 3.75 m; from the pronaos eleven steps down to a platform 3.66 m above the area, with a railing, two narrow stairs at its ends. These are the Augustan remains, drawn for the temple of Metellus (117 BC) on the same site
unverified: the 117 BC temple drawn with the Augustan dimensions

QFr. 2.3.6; Plut. Sulla 33); standards of weights and measures kept in it
monuments.geometry_source: Platner-Ashby s.v. Castor, Aedes (Augustan temple c. 50 x 30 m, floor 7 m above the Sacra Via, octastyle peripteral, 11 columns on each side, 12.5 m columns; podium of Metellus 117 BC on the same site); facing north onto the Forum
monuments.location: south side of the Forum, beside the Vicus Tuscus
monuments.notes: CORRECTED: the dedication day was 27 January (calendar), not 15 July (15 July is the transvectio equitum linked to the Lake Regillus apparition, Dion. Hal. 6.13) (P&A: 'The day of dedication is given in the calendar as 27th January'). P&A: vowed 499 by the dictator A. Postumius, dedicated 484 by his son as duumvir (Liv. 2.20.12, 2.42.5); restored 117 by L. Caecilius Metellus (Cic. Scaur. 46; Verr. 2.1.129-154); completely rebuilt by Tiberius in AD 6 (outside our range). The octastyle peripteral temple (11 columns on the flanks, podium floor about 7 m above the Sacra Via, platform 3.66 m above the area) is the Augustan/Tiberian building, not the republican one. Standard weights and measures kept in it. Pleiades 157276290; the placement here is moved to it.

Cam. 21; Livy 5.40.7 itself says the Vestals carried the sacra away), again in 241 when L. Caecilius Metellus saved the Palladium (Liv. Per. 19; Plin. NH 7.141); saved from the fire of 210 by thirteen slaves (Livy 26.27.2); burned AD 64. The later temple was of white marble with 20 columns; the surviving concrete podium has a foundation 15.05 m across. Pleiades 55302071.

Excavations show remains of the republican house immediately south of the temple, adjoining the Domus Publica on the east, 'though almost no remains earlier than the second century BC are now visible'. The 'built -509 regal period' was an assumption, replaced. Livy 26.27.1-14 (210 fire) refers to the 'atrium regium', not the Vestals' house. Surviving structure is Neronian-Severan. Pleiades 795139357.

built.by: house said to have been built by Numa Pompilius (Plut. Numa 14; Solin. 1.21; Ov. Trist. 3.1.30); cappellaccio walls older than the Gallic fire of 390 (P&A)

Domitius Calvinus rebuilt it in marble (Dio 48.42.4); a possible burning by the Gauls in 390; cappellaccio walls from before 390. Principal part trapezoidal, mean 22 x 8 m, white marble blocks (Calvinus phase). Contained the sacrarium of Mars (hastae and ancilia: Serv. Aen. 7.603; Gell. 4.6; Dio 44.17). Livy 26.27.2 names an 'atrium regium' among the buildings burned in 210; P&A's Regia article does not list a 210 fire, so that event is flagged uncertain. Pontifex Maximus's residence moved by Augustus in 12 BC (Dio 54.27). Pleiades 554680094. The 'sacra of Mars and Ops' in the old form field: the Mars shrine is verified, Ops is not in P&A's text and was dropped.

built.by: tradition: vowed by L. Furius Camillus in 367 during the Licinian-Sextian disturbances (Plut. Cam. 42; Ov. Fast. 1.641-644); actual date of erection unknown (P&A)

monuments.notes: CORRECTED: certainty lowered to traditional. P&A: temple at the north-west corner of the forum 'said to have been vowed by L. Furius Camillus in 367' (Plut. Cam. 42; Varro LL 5.148, 5.156; Ov. Fast. 1.641-644); 'the date of the actual erection of the temple is not known'; dedication day probably 22 July. Statue of Victory on its roof struck by lightning 211 (Livy 26.23.4). After the death of C. Gracchus the Senate ordered L. Opimius to restore it, 121 (Plut. C. Gracchus 17; App. BC 1.26). The aedicula of Concord set up on the Graecostasis by the aedile Cn. Flavius in 304 (Livy 9.46.6) is a separate small shrine. P&A also lists a separate temple of Concordia on the Arx (vowed 218 by the praetor L. Manlius, dedicated 5 Feb 216: Livy 22.33.7, 23.21.7), which is not in this dataset. Aen. 1.291). Doors closed in 235 after the First Punic War (Livy 1.19.3), 'in 30 B.C. after Actium' per P&A (Hor. Carm. 4.15.9), and twice more by Augustus (Mon. Anc. 2.42-46 = RG 13; Suet. Aug. 22). built.by: legend, three versions: M. Curtius leaps into the chasm in 362 (Livy 7.6); Mettius Curtius in the Sabine war (Livy 1.12.10; Varro LL 5.149-150); or the spot enclosed by the consul C. Curtius in 445 (Varro LL 5.150)

monuments.form: irregular trapezoidal paved field about 10 m x 9 m; extant layers of cappellaccio and Monte Verde tufa (Sullan period) with a travertine layer from the Caesarian reconstruction; a dry shrine by Augustus's time
monuments.geometry_source: Platner-Ashby s.v. Lacus Curtius (trapezoidal paved field about 10 m long and 9 m wide, third layer of travertine with a curb)
monuments.location: middle of the Forum
monuments.notes: P&A gives three explanations of the name: (1) the Sabine Mettius Curtius who rode into the marsh in the war of Romulus and Tatius (Livy 1.12.10; Varro LL 5.149); (2) the leap of M. Curtius into a chasm, 362 BC (Livy 7.6.1-6; relief in Palazzo dei Conservatori, a late copy of a c. 2nd-c. original); (3) a spot struck by lightning and enclosed by C. Curtius, consul 445 (Varro LL 5.150). By Augustus it was dry ground (Ov. Fast. 6.403-404). Existing remains: two layers of cappellaccio and Monte Verde tufa attributed to the Sullan period (Van Deman, Frank) with a travertine layer from the Caesarian reconstruction, about 10 m x 9 m. The year 362 is therefore one of three legendary dates, not a historical fact. Pleiades 459049147 (precise).

built.by: early; water where Castor and Pollux watered horses after Lake Regillus (Dion. Hal. 6.13)

No building date given: the basin (about 10 m square at the top, 2.12 m deep) is a later structure over an earlier tufa pavement; coins of the gens Postumia (c. 90 BC) show the spring as a puteal with the Dioscuri. The temple of Castor was built on the west side of the spring. Pleiades 707467453 (precise) adopted for coordinates.

built.by: the Carcer ascribed to Ancus Marcius (Livy 1.33.8); the lower chamber (Tullianum) to Servius Tullius (Varro LL 5.151; Festus 356); T. Frank dates the lower chamber to the 3rd c. BC (P&A, disputed)

monuments.notes: Verified: P&A: honorary arch at the east end of the forum over the Sacra Via, erected by Q. Fabius Allobrogicus in 121 after his victory over the Allobroges (Cic. Planc. 17; de Or. 2.267; Verr. 1.19); the first arch of its kind in or near the forum; restored by his grandson in 56 (CIL I2 763 = VI 1304). The surviving voussoirs may be from it. Not in Pleiades.

built.by: erected in 338 BC in honour of C. Maenius, the victor in the naval battle at Antium (Plin. NH 34.20); another tradition, probably false, made it the column a later Maenius kept when he sold his house to Cato for the Basilica Porcia (Asc. in Cic. div. in Caec. 50). Platner-Ashby s.v. Columna Maenia, read

monuments.form: an honorific column; still standing in the 4th century AD (Symm. Ep. 5.54.3); a time-signal mark: when the setting sun moved from it to the Carcer the last hour was called (Plin. NH 7.212)
monuments.geometry_source: site only (Platner-Ashby s.v. Columna Maenia, read); height and order assumed
monuments.location: on the north-west side of the Forum, near the Basilica Porcia and the Carcer
monuments.notes: Added in U8 as part of the Forum's furniture. Its exact spot is unknown (near the Basilica Porcia and the Carcer); the statue on top is assumed from the honour of a column (Pliny NH 34.20), not stated by Platner-Ashby.

built.by: erected by the consul C. Duilius after the naval victory over Carthage at Mylae in 260 (Pliny NH 34.20; Quint. 1.7.12; Serv. Georg. 3.29); the surviving inscription is a later restoration (c. 150 BC or imperial)

monuments.geometry_source: Plin. NH 34.20; Platner-Ashby s.v. Columna Rostrata C. Duilii (a column with ships beaks); height assumed, site rough
monuments.location: Forum, near the Rostra
monuments.notes: P&A: C. Duilius erected two columnae rostratae after his naval victory over the Carthaginians in 260; one stood 'ante circum a parte ianuarium' (Serv. Georg. 3.29), the second and more famous stood on or near the Rostra; its archaic inscription was restored about 150 BC and again under Augustus (CIL I2 25) or Tiberius/Claudius; part of the inscription (CIL VI 1300 = 31591) is in the Palazzo dei Conservatori. built.by: Q. Lutatius Catulus as consul 78 (CIL VI 1313 inscription)

monuments.form: huge substructure and archive building on the Capitoline slope above the Forum: a 3.43 m thick foundation wall with six window recesses, a first-storey corridor 5 m wide and 10 m high, and an arcade of eleven arches with engaged Doric half-columns of peperino; outer walls of sperone (Gabine stone), inner walls of Anio tufa
monuments.geometry_source: Platner-Ashby s.v. Tabularium (substructure wall 3.43 m thick, first-storey corridor 5 m wide and 10 high, eleven arches 7.5 m high and 3.5-3.6 wide; length c. 70 m in the kit, Platner gives no length); front faces the Forum (ESE)
monuments.location: Capitol, between the two summits, facing the Forum
monuments.notes: CORRECTED citation: the inscriptions are CIL I2 737 = VI 1314 (copied by Signorili and Poggio) and CIL I2 736 = VI 1133 = 31597 (P&A); 'CIL VI 1313' was wrong. Q. Lutatius Catulus (consul 78) 'substructionem et tabularium de s(enatus) s(ententia) faciundum coeravit eidemque probavit'. P&A: substructio wall 3.43 m thick with six recesses and narrow windows; first-story corridor 5 m wide, 10 m high; front an arcade of eleven arches (7.50 m high, 3.54-3.60 m wide) with engaged Doric half-columns of peperino; outer walls sperone (Gabine stone), inner walls Anio tufa, bases and imposts travertine. Second story added or rebuilt c. end of the 1st century (AD). Not in Pleiades.

built.by: existed by 212 BC (Livy 25.7.12); restored and enlarged by the censors of 194 (Livy 34.44.5); magnificently rebuilt by C. Asinius Pollio (Suet. Aug. 29; Pliny NH 7.115), probably after 39 BC

events.what: restored and enlarged by the censors together with the Villa Publica (Livy 34.44.5)

monuments.location: Capitol slope above the Forum of Caesar / Forum of Augustus
monuments.notes: CORRECTED: the old text claimed Livy 43.16.13 records a rebuilding in 169 by Gracchus and Claudius; in the Latin text it only has the censors going up into the atrium Libertatis and sealing the tablets and closing the tabularium (169) when put on trial. P&A: building holding the censors' offices and records and some bronze laws (Livy 43.16, 45.15; Festus 241); said to have held the Thurian hostages in 212 (Livy 25.7.12) and slaves tortured at Milo's trial (Cic. Mil. 59); restored and enlarged by the censors of 194 (Livy 34.44.5, 'atrium Libertatis et villa publica ab iisdem refecta amplificataque'); restored magnificently by Asinius Pollio (Suet. Aug. 29; the usual date 39 BC is not in the P&A text read here). The earlier claim 'existed by 214 (Livy 24.18)' is unsupported and was removed. Site unknown (not on the later curia site). Not in Pleiades.

monuments.location: from the Forum (below the Basilica Aemilia) through the Velabrum to the Tiber near the Pons Aemilius
monuments.notes: CORRECTED: Livy 39.44.5 (Latin text): the censors Cato and Flaccus (184) let contracts to clean the sewers and to make NEW sewers on the Aventine and elsewhere; it is not about 'covered sewers'. Livy 1.38.6 (verified in Latin): Tarquinius Priscus drained the low ground round the forum with sewers; P&A: tradition ascribes the Cloaca Maxima to Tarquinius Superbus (Liv. 1.56.2; Dion. Hal. 3.67.5, 4.44.1; Strabo 5.3.8). P&A: it began as a stream regulated by walls, probably not roofed until after the Tarquins (Plaut. Curc. 476 'canalis'); nothing of the original drain survives except perhaps a short cappellaccio section under the Basilica Aemilia; most existing parts date from the 3rd c. BC or later; the channel near the Forum is 4.20 m high and 3.20 m wide. Agrippa inspected it as aedile in 33 BC (Pliny NH 36.104; Dio 49.43.1 not checked). Pleiades 867802692 (precise) is the outfall near S. Giorgio in Velabro.

built.by: name derived from Etruscans given land to live there after Porsenna's war (Livy 2.14.9), or from Caeles Vibenna's followers (P&A); no building date

Hal. 5.36.4); eastern boundary of the Velabrum. The name is derived from Etruscans, either fled from Porsenna (Livy 2.14.9, verified: 'locus ad habitandum datus quem deinde Tuscum vicum appellarunt') or from the followers of Caeles Vibenna. Pleiades 380281017.

monuments.notes: P&A: the cattle market of Rome (Cic. Scaur. 23; Dion. Hal. 1.40, 4.27), extending from the boundary of the Velabrum to the Tiber; monuments include the two fornices of L. Stertinius (196 BC), the Busta Gallica and Doliola (probably primitive tombs). Pleiades 207271756.

built.by: Evander, according to tradition (Livy 1.7.3-15)

monuments.location: Forum Boarium, near the Circus Maximus end; under S. Maria in Cosmedin
monuments.notes: P&A: earliest cult centre of Hercules in Rome, raised, by tradition, after Hercules slew Cacus and Evander recognised his divinity (Livy 1.7.10-11; Dion. Hal. 1.40.6; Fest. 237; Serv. Aen. 8.269-271); one tradition ascribes the dedication to Evander (Dion. Hal.; Macrob. 3.11.7). Livy 9.29.9: Appius Claudius's censorship (312) hands the rites to public slaves. Burned in Nero's fire (Tac. Ann. 15.41) but restored. Site north-west of the probable ara; relations between the Hercules shrines 'by no means clear'. Pleiades 207271757 has only a 'related' location, not adopted.
sources: Platner-Ashby s.v. Hercules Invictus, Ara Maxima

built.by: both temples ascribed to Servius Tullius (Livy 33.27.4; Dion. Hal. 4.27); Mater Matuta vowed by Camillus 396 and dedicated 396/395 (Livy 5.19.6, 5.23.7; P&A 395)

monuments.english: Temples of Fortuna and Mater Matuta

events.what: temple of Mater Matuta vowed or dedicated by M. Furius Camillus after the capture of Veii (Livy 5.19.6, 5.23.7); P&A gives 395
both temples burned (Livy 24.47.15); restored the next year (Livy 25.7.6)
L. Stertinius sets up two arches with gilded statues before the temples (Livy 33.27.4)

monuments.geometry_source: Platner-Ashby s.v. Aedes Matris Matutae / Fortunae (the temple at S. Omobono: archaeology of two temples side by side, same orientation, the Ionic tetrastyle pseudoperipteral one 20 x 12 m on a podium 2.5 m high, orientation N-S parallel with the Tiber for the Pons Aemilius temple, which faced the street from the Pons Aemilius); east assumed for the archaic pair
monuments.location: Forum Boarium, Sant'Omobono precinct
monuments.notes: P&A treats two temples side by side (Fortuna and Mater Matuta) in the Forum Boarium just inside the Porta Carmentalis (Liv. 25.7.6): both ascribed by tradition to Servius Tullius; Mater Matuta restored and dedicated by Camillus in 395 (P&A; Livy 5.19.6: Camillus vows to dedicate the rebuilt temple of Mater Matuta, 'iam ante ab rege Ser. Tullio dedicatam'; Livy 5.23.7: he dedicates it, in the year Livy gives as 396); both burned in 213 (Livy 24.47.15) and restored the next year by commissioners (Livy 25.7.6); in 196 L. Stertinius set up two arches with gilded statues in front of them (Livy 33.27.4); dedication day for both 11 June (Matralia). P&A (1929) identifies the Ionic temple converted into S. Maria Egiziaca with Mater Matuta (far from certain) and knows nothing of the S. Omobono area excavation (1937 on) with its 6th-c. temples, which is the modern basis for the coordinates (Pleiades 103123065). Fortuna's archaic wooden statue (Ov. Fast. 6.569-580; Dion. Hal. 4.40) was undamaged by the fire.
sources: Platner-Ashby s.v. Fortuna, Aedes; Mater Matuta, Aedes

built.by: a round temple of Hercules in the Forum Boarium existed by 296 (Livy 10.23.3); a temple of Hercules Victor vowed 145 and dedicated 142 by L. Mummius (CIL I2 626 = VI 331, P&A), perhaps the same or a rebuilding

monuments.english: Round Temple in the Forum Boarium (Hercules Victor)

events.what: Mummius dedicates a temple and statue of Hercules Victor (CIL I2 626 = VI 331; whether this is the round temple is uncertain)

monuments.form: round temple in the Forum Boarium; the surviving marble round temple has 20 Corinthian columns and a cella 10 m in diameter on a 2 m tufa podium with a republican favissa (P&A describes it under Portunus); identification with Hercules Victor is modern, P&A prefers Portunus
monuments.geometry_source: Platner-Ashby s.v. Hercules Victor (circular, 20 Corinthian columns, Greek marble); radius c. 7.4 m (14.8 m across, as in the kit)
monuments.location: Forum Boarium, by the Tiber
monuments.notes: CORRECTED: 'Vitr. 3.2.5 (Hermodorus of Salamis)' removed: Vitruvius 3.2.5 names Hermodorus as architect of the temple of Mars in the Circus Flaminius (and the Jupiter Stator temple), not this round temple; the Hermodorus attribution here is a modern guess, not an ancient source. P&A: Hercules Victor, a round temple in the Forum Boarium already standing in 296 BC (Livy 10.23.3 'ad aedem rotundam Herculis'), with frescoes by the poet Pacuvius (Plin. NH 35.19); a temple of Hercules Victor was vowed by L. Mummius in 145 and dedicated in 142 as censor, to judge from CIL I2 626 = VI 331 (found on the Caelian, so the connection to this round temple is not certain); a possible restoration by L. Aemilius Paullus rests on a conjectural emendation of Festus 242 (P&A). P&A also says the remains destroyed under Sixtus IV were a round temple near S. Maria in Cosmedin and that the surviving round temple (S. Maria del Sole) is, 'more probably', the temple of Portunus; modern scholarship reverses this (Hercules Victor = the round temple, Portunus = the rectangular Ionic temple). The marble round temple (c. 120 BC) is a modern dating, not in P&A, and is kept only as a flagged guess. Pleiades 825969667 (Temple of Hercules Victor) adopted for coordinates.
sources: Platner-Ashby s.v. Hercules Victor, Aedes; Portunium

built.by: temple of Portunus 'in portu Tiberino' near the Pons Aemilius, dedicated on 17 August (Varro LL 6.19; fasti); founding date unknown

monuments.form: the rectangular Ionic tetrastyle prostyle temple (about 20 x 12 m on a 2.5 m podium) is the modern identification, dated by modern scholars to the late 2nd or early 1st c. BC; P&A prefers the round temple
monuments.geometry_source: Platner-Ashby s.v. Aedes Portuni (tetrastyle Ionic pseudoperipteral on a podium); front toward the Tiber assumed
monuments.location: Forum Boarium, by the Tiber beside the round temple
monuments.notes: CORRECTED: the old '-120 probable, extant tetrastyle Ionic temple' was unsupported. P&A: Varro LL 6.19: 'Portunalia dicta a Portuno, cui eo die aedes in portu Tiberino facta et feriae institutae'; Portunalia on 17 August = dedication day, calendar 'Portuno ad pontem Aemilium'; the portus Tiberinus is a quay near the Pons Aemilius, temple close by; no date. P&A thinks the round temple (S. Maria del Sole) is probably Portunus, far from certain, and identifies the rectangular Ionic tetrastyle prostyle temple (S. Maria Egiziaca, 20 x 12 m, podium 2.5 m) as Mater Matuta, which cannot be reconciled with the modern identification used here for coordinates (Pleiades 494660670: the rectangular temple); the c. 120-80 BC date of that building is modern (not in P&A) and flagged.

built.by: gate on the line of the Servian Wall (wall completed 378: Livy 6.32.1); the gate is named already in 439 (Livy 4.16.2)

monuments.geometry_source: Platner-Ashby s.v. Porta Trigemina (an arch of tufa, 3.30 m wide, over a paved road found 40 m south of S. Maria in Cosmedin); flanking towers assumed
monuments.location: Servian Wall, between the Capitol/Forum Boarium and the Tiber
monuments.notes: CORRECTED: the gate existed in the story of 439 (Livy 4.16.2: L. Minucius given an ox 'extra portam Trigeminam'), before the wall of 378, so '378 certain' is unsound; the name, if not anachronistic in Livy, implies a gate on the Palatine-Aventine line before the Servian Wall. P&A: important gate in the Servian wall between the Aventine and the Tiber (Region XI), exact site disputed: below S. Sabina, or about 40 m south of S. Maria in Cosmedin (arch of tufa 3.30 m wide found 1886), or at the north corner of the Aventine near S. Anna dei Calzettari. Livy 35.10.12 (193 BC): the aediles built a portico outside the Porta Trigemina and added the Emporium to it; Livy 41.27.8 (174): the censors paved the Emporium outside the gate, repaired the Porticus Aemilia and paved a portico inside the gate up the Aventine. Pleiades 303638861 has only a 'related' location.

built.by: early market (Livy 21.62.3)

monuments.form: open market about 125 x 40-50 m (once enclosed), paved with travertine by the 2nd c. BC; four temples (Pietas, Janus, Spes, Juno Sospita) and later the Theatre of Marcellus around it
monuments.geometry_source: vegetable market north of the Theatre of Marcellus; extent assumed (Platner-Ashby s.v. Forum Holitorium)
monuments.location: below the south slope of the Capitol by the Tiber; later under the Theatre of Marcellus
monuments.notes: P&A: the vegetable market, just outside the Porta Carmentalis (Varro LL 5.146; 'hoc erat antiquum macellum'), south-east and north-east limits formed by the Servian wall and the Capitoline slope; later enclosed by four temples (Pietas, Janus, Spes, Juno Sospita) and the Theatre of Marcellus; paved by the 2nd c. BC; the built-up forum was about 125 x 40-50 m. Livy 21.62.3 (218 BC prodigy: an ox climbed to the third floor from the Forum Boarium; the vegetable market is named in the same passage) was not verified in detail. Pleiades 72845305.

built.by: C. Duilius, after Mylae (Tac. Ann. 2.49); dedication day 17 August (fasti)

monuments.geometry_source: Platner-Ashby s.v. Aedes Iani: three temples side by side with the same orientation facing the Forum Holitorium
monuments.location: Forum Holitorium, next to Spes and Juno Sospita
monuments.notes: Not in Pleiades as a separate place. P&A: temple in the forum Holitorium built by C. Duilius after Mylae (Tac. Ann. 2.49), ad theatrum Marcelli (Fast. Allif.), extra portam Carmentalem (Fest. 285); dedication day 17 August; restoration begun by Augustus, completed by Tiberius AD 17 (outside range). Augustus placed a statue of Janus from Egypt in it (Plin. NH 36.28). The three temples under S. Nicola in Carcere (Pleiades church point 41.8911, 12.4799) cannot be assigned individually with certainty: P&A (1929) tentatively follows Delbrueck/Frank (south = Spes; central = about 90 BC; Doric 'smallest' = Juno Sospita), while later scholarship generally calls the northern Doric one Janus and the central Ionic one Juno Sospita; coordinates here are therefore at the church only.

Ann. 2.49); struck by lightning 218 (Livy 21.62.4); burned 213 and restored next year by a commission (Livy 24.47.15-16, 25.7.6); burned again in 31 (Dio 50.10.3); rebuilt later (Germanicus dedicated AD 17); dedication day 1 August. built.by: vowed by C. Cornelius Cethegus 197 against the Insubres; dedicated 194 (Livy 32.30.10, 34.53.3)

Cornelius Cethegus in the Insubrian war (Livy 32.30.10) and dedicated in 194 (Livy 34.53.3; P&A's text prints '104', a misprint) on 1 February; restored by L. Julius (Caesar), consul 90, after Cornelia's dream (Cic. Div. 1.4, 1.99; Obseq. 75). Not in Pleiades. The three temples under S. built.by: vowed by M'. Acilius Glabrio at Thermopylae in 191; dedicated in 181 by his son, duumvir (Livy 40.34.5)

monuments.location: Forum Holitorium
monuments.notes: Verified: P&A: vowed by M'. Acilius Glabrio at Thermopylae (191), begun by him, dedicated in 181 by his son as duumvir (Livy 40.34.4-5; the Latin text reads 'altera in foro holitorio Pietatis; eam aedem dedicauit M'. Acilius Glabrio duumuir', with the first gilded statue in Italy for his father); at the east end of the area later occupied by the Theatre of Marcellus; destroyed by Caesar in 44 for the theatre (Plin. NH 7.121). Dedication day 1 December per fasti is for the other (Circus Flaminius) temple of Pietas, not this one. Not in Pleiades.

built.by: vowed by Ap. Claudius Caecus in battle against Etruscans and Samnites in 296 (Livy 10.19.17-21; Plin. NH 35.12); dedicated a few years later, on 3 June (Ov. Fast. 6.201)
